profileSections.summary: Jarrah is a Western Australian tree recorded by Florabase to about 40 metres high.
profileSections.identifying_features: Rough fibrous bark is a major field character. Florabase records white to cream flowers, sometimes pink-toned.
profileSections.habitat: Recorded on grey sand, clay, sandy loam and laterite, especially on hills and rises.
profileSections.phenology: Flowering is recorded from June through December, sometimes extending into January.
profileSections.distribution: Native to Western Australia and strongly associated with the south-west.
profileSections.conservation_status: Florabase lists the taxon as not threatened in Western Australia.
profileSections.data_quality: Florabase name and descriptive fields were curated into ArbotFlash on 17 June 2026. A global-backbone and APC cross-check remains pending.

profileSections.summary: Marri is usually a large tree, although Florabase notes that it can rarely occur as a mallee.
profileSections.identifying_features: The bark is rough and tessellated. White or pink flowers and large woody fruits are useful field characters.
profileSections.habitat: It occupies a broad range of south-western settings including flats, hills, slopes, breakaways, wetlands and drainage lines on varied soils.
profileSections.phenology: Flowering is recorded from December or January through May.
profileSections.distribution: Native to Western Australia and widespread through much of the south-west.
profileSections.conservation_status: Florabase lists the taxon as not threatened in Western Australia.
profileSections.exudates: Marri can produce conspicuous red kino. This is retained as botanical exudate information only, with no grip-product content.
profileSections.data_quality: Florabase name and descriptive fields were curated into ArbotFlash on 17 June 2026. A global-backbone and APC cross-check remains pending.

profileSections.summary: Tuart is a coastal eucalypt recorded by Florabase as a tree about 10–40 metres high.
profileSections.identifying_features: Florabase describes rough, box-type bark and white flowers.
profileSections.habitat: Characteristically associated with coastal plains and sand over limestone.
profileSections.phenology: Flowering is recorded from January to April.
profileSections.distribution: Florabase records native and naturalised occurrences, including the Swan Coastal Plain, Geraldton Sandplains and Esperance Plains.
profileSections.conservation_status: Florabase lists the taxon as not threatened in Western Australia.
profileSections.data_quality: Florabase name and descriptive fields were curated into ArbotFlash on 17 June 2026. The mixed native/naturalised status is preserved rather than simplified.

profileSections.summary: Karri is a very tall south-western eucalypt; Florabase records trees from about 10 metres to as much as 90 metres.
profileSections.identifying_features: The trunk is characteristically smooth-barked and the flowers are white.
profileSections.habitat: Recorded on sandy loam, particularly on hillsides.
profileSections.phenology: Florabase records flowering in May or from September through summer into February.
profileSections.distribution: Native to Western Australia, especially the high-rainfall south-west and Warren region.
profileSections.conservation_status: Florabase lists the taxon as not threatened in Western Australia.
profileSections.data_quality: Florabase name and descriptive fields were curated into ArbotFlash on 17 June 2026.

profileSections.summary: Wandoo is a smooth-barked Western Australian tree recorded to about 25 metres high.
profileSections.identifying_features: The bark is smooth and may be powdery or non-powdery; flowers are white to cream.
profileSections.habitat: Recorded on sandy and clay loams, gravel, laterite and granite, often on stony rises and undulating country.
profileSections.phenology: Flowering is recorded from December or January through May.
profileSections.distribution: Native across several south-western bioregions, including the Avon Wheatbelt, Jarrah Forest and Swan Coastal Plain.
profileSections.conservation_status: Florabase lists the taxon as not threatened in Western Australia.
profileSections.data_quality: Florabase name and descriptive fields were curated into ArbotFlash on 17 June 2026.

profileSections.summary: WA peppermint is a tree or shrub recorded by Florabase to about 10 metres high.
profileSections.identifying_features: The species has a characteristically weeping habit and white flowers; its foliage is aromatic when crushed.
profileSections.habitat: Recorded on white or grey sand, sandy soils, laterite and limestone in coastal dunes, granite outcrops and limestone areas.
profileSections.phenology: Flowering is recorded from July through December.
profileSections.distribution: Florabase records both native and naturalised occurrences in Western Australia.
profileSections.conservation_status: Florabase lists the taxon as not threatened in Western Australia.
profileSections.data_quality: Florabase name and descriptive fields were curated into ArbotFlash on 17 June 2026. The mixed establishment status is retained.

profileSections.summary: Western sheoak is a dioecious tree recorded by Florabase at about 5–15 metres high.
profileSections.identifying_features: The bark is fibrous and reddish-brown. Male and female reproductive structures occur on separate plants.
profileSections.habitat: Recorded on lateritic soils and white, grey or yellow sands in jarrah forest and sand-dune habitats.
profileSections.phenology: Flowering is recorded from May through October.
profileSections.distribution: Native to Western Australia, particularly the Jarrah Forest, Swan Coastal Plain and Warren bioregions.
profileSections.conservation_status: Florabase lists the taxon as not threatened in Western Australia.

profileSections.summary: Banksia attenuata is a lignotuberous tree or shrub, ranging from low shrubby forms to trees around 10 metres high.
profileSections.identifying_features: Bright yellow cylindrical flower spikes and narrow leaves are prominent features. Florabase records both lignotuberous and epicormic recovery structures.
profileSections.habitat: Recorded mainly on white, yellow, brown or pale red sands, sometimes over laterite, on dunes and sandplains.
profileSections.phenology: Flowering is recorded from October through summer, sometimes extending into February.
profileSections.distribution: Native to Western Australia and widespread across much of the south-west.
profileSections.conservation_status: Florabase lists the taxon as not threatened in Western Australia.
profileSections.fire_response: Florabase identifies a lignotuber and epicormic buds, supporting resprouting after fire.
profileSections.data_quality: Florabase name and descriptive fields were curated into ArbotFlash on 17 June 2026.

source.citation: Western Australian Herbarium (1998–). Florabase—the Western Australian flora. Taxon profile 1800, accessed 17 June 2026.

profileSections.summary: The Western Australian Christmas tree is a woody root hemiparasite recorded as a tree or shrub to about 10 metres high.
profileSections.identifying_features: Rough grey-brown bark and masses of yellow-orange flowers in late spring and early summer make it highly distinctive.
profileSections.habitat: Recorded on many sandy, gravelly and rocky substrates across sandplains, slopes and the bases of rock outcrops.
profileSections.phenology: Flowering is recorded from October through December or January.
profileSections.distribution: Native to Western Australia and recorded across a broad spread of south-western bioregions.
profileSections.conservation_status: Florabase lists the taxon as not threatened in Western Australia.
profileSections.ecology: The plant forms haustorial root connections to host plants and remains photosynthetic, so it is represented as a root hemiparasite rather than a wholly non-photosynthetic parasite.
profileSections.data_quality: Florabase name and descriptive fields were curated into ArbotFlash on 17 June 2026.

source.citation: Western Australian Herbarium (1998–). Florabase—the Western Australian flora. Taxon profile 2401, accessed 17 June 2026.

profileSections.summary: Xanthorrhoea preissii is a perennial tree-like monocot recorded to about 5 metres high, with a trunk that can exceed 3 metres.
profileSections.identifying_features: A dense crown of narrow leaves sits above a dark trunk, and the flowering scape carries a long cream-white spike.
profileSections.habitat: Recorded on sands, loams, gravelly sandy clay, laterite and granite across ranges, the coastal plain and areas near watercourses.
profileSections.phenology: Flowering is recorded in June or from August through December.
profileSections.distribution: Native to Western Australia and widespread through several south-western bioregions.
profileSections.conservation_status: Florabase lists the taxon as not threatened in Western Australia.
profileSections.exudates: The species can produce resinous exudate. ArbotFlash retains this as botanical and historical information only.
profileSections.data_quality: Florabase name and descriptive fields were curated into ArbotFlash on 17 June 2026.

profileSections.summary: Raspberry Jam Wattle is a woody shrub or tree recorded from about 1 to 7 metres high, occasionally reaching about 12 metres.
profileSections.identifying_features: Its yellow flowering display is recorded from July to October. Florabase notes that it occupies a broad variety of soils and habitats.
profileSections.habitat: Recorded across varied soils and habitats rather than being restricted to one substrate type.
profileSections.phenology: Flowering is recorded from July through October.
profileSections.distribution: Florabase records a broad Western Australian range across numerous inland and south-western bioregions, including the Avon Wheatbelt, Jarrah Forest and Swan Coastal Plain.
profileSections.conservation_status: Florabase lists the taxon as not threatened in Western Australia and as native in part of its range but naturalised elsewhere.

profileSections.summary: Coastal Wattle is usually a dense shrub and only occasionally a small tree, generally 0.8 to 4 metres high and sometimes about 7 metres.
profileSections.identifying_features: Florabase records yellow flowers and a dense coastal growth form. The selected diagnostic image shows the distinctive curved pods and conspicuous red-orange seed arils.
profileSections.habitat: Associated with white or grey sand, coastal dunes and limestone.
profileSections.phenology: Flowering is recorded from September to December and may also occur from January to May.
profileSections.distribution: Native to Western Australia, especially coastal and near-coastal regions spanning the south-west and south coast.
profileSections.conservation_status: Florabase lists the taxon as not threatened in Western Australia.

profileSections.identifying_features: Large divided leaves and broad yellow-green flower spikes are prominent characters. Florabase records epicormic buds.
profileSections.habitat: Recorded on white or grey sand and laterite.
profileSections.phenology: Flowering is recorded mainly from September to December, sometimes extending into January.
profileSections.distribution: Occurs in the South-west Botanical Province across bioregions including the Jarrah Forest, Swan Coastal Plain and Warren.

profileSections.summary: Holly-leaf Banksia is an erect tree or shrub reaching about 12 metres high.
profileSections.identifying_features: Holly-like lobed leaves and flower heads that can shift through cream, yellow, orange and red are strong field characters. Florabase records epicormic buds.
profileSections.habitat: Found on white or grey sand, black sandy loam, limestone, granite or quartz, including consolidated dunes and low-lying flats.
profileSections.phenology: Florabase records flowering across much of the year.
profileSections.distribution: Native to Western Australia and associated with the south-west.
profileSections.conservation_status: Florabase lists the taxon as not threatened in Western Australia.

profileSections.summary: Acorn Banksia is a non-lignotuberous tree or shrub reaching about 10 metres high.
profileSections.identifying_features: Cream-and-orange flower spikes and deeply toothed leaves are prominent field characters. Florabase specifically describes the taxon as non-lignotuberous.
profileSections.habitat: Recorded on several sandy and gravelly substrates, sandy loam, brown clay, laterite and granite, especially on sandplains, dunes and undulating slopes.
profileSections.phenology: Flowering is recorded from February through August.
profileSections.distribution: Occurs across both the Eremaean and South-west Botanical Provinces, including the Swan Coastal Plain, Geraldton Sandplains and Avon Wheatbelt.
profileSections.conservation_status: Florabase lists the taxon as not threatened in Western Australia.

profileSections.phenology: Flowering is recorded in December or from January through April.
profileSections.distribution: Native to Western Australia and recorded in the Avon Wheatbelt, Geraldton Sandplains, Jarrah Forest and Swan Coastal Plain.
profileSections.conservation_status: Florabase lists the taxon as not threatened in Western Australia.

profileSections.summary: Swan River Blackbutt is a tree generally 3 to 25 metres high.
profileSections.identifying_features: The bark is rough and longitudinally furrowed, making the trunk a strong diagnostic feature. Flowers are white to cream.
profileSections.habitat: Recorded on gravelly soils, sandy clay and loam in depressions, stream banks and valleys.
profileSections.phenology: Flowering is recorded in July and August and again from November through February.
profileSections.distribution: Native to Western Australia and recorded in the Jarrah Forest, Swan Coastal Plain and Warren bioregions.
profileSections.conservation_status: Florabase lists the taxon as not threatened in Western Australia.
